title: False Claims Act enacted ('Lincoln Law')
description: Congress passed the False Claims Act during the Civil War against fraud by defence contractors; it lets private citizens sue on the government's behalf (qui tam) and share in the recovery.
quote: a federal statute originally enacted in 1863 in response to defense contractor fraud during the American Civil War

title: False Claims Act enacted (Civil War)
description: Act of March 2, 1863 (12 Stat. 696) let any person sue in the name of the United States to recover penalties for frauds on the government; the relator received half of the recovery.
quote: The False Claims Act originated as the Act of March 2, 1863.

title: Original informant-reward law
description: The authority now in section 7623(a) originates in an 1867 law allowing the Treasury to pay sums for detecting and punishing tax violators.
location: printed p. 1 (PDF p. 3), Prior Law and Policy
quote: What is now section 7623(a) ... of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) has its origins in legislation enacted in 1867.

title: 1943 amendments curtail qui tam
description: After the Attorney General sought repeal, Congress instead cut relator shares (max 25%, or 10% if the government took the case), required relators to hand over their evidence, gave the government 60 days to intervene, and barred suits based on information already in government hands (Pub. L. 78-213, 57 Stat. 608).
quote: The two Houses ultimately reached agreement and passed the compromise as Public Law 78-213.

title: BSA informant rewards enacted
description: 31 U.S.C. 5323 'Rewards for informants' lets Treasury pay up to 25 percent (max $150,000) for information leading to BSA recoveries over $50,000.
quote: (Added Pub. L. 98–473, title II, §901(e), Oct. 12, 1984, 98 Stat. 2135.)

title: False Claims Amendments Act of 1986
description: The 1986 amendments revived qui tam suits: a relator gets 15-25% of the proceeds when the government takes over the case and 25-30% when the relator goes it alone.

title: False Claims Amendments Act of 1986
description: Pub. L. 99-562 revived qui tam: relator shares of 15-25% (government intervenes) or 25-30% (government declines), treble damages, higher penalties, anti-retaliation protection, and a new public-disclosure bar with an original-source exception. Qui tam filings rose from 31 new matters in FY1987 to hundreds a year.
quote: To amend title 31, United States Code, with respect to the fraudulent use of public property or money.

title: Financial Institutions Anti-Fraud Enforcement Act of 1990
